claim: Urodeles deviate from anurans and amniotes in that their limbs exhibit preaxial skeletal differentiation.
source: Here, we investigated how Sonic hedgehog (Shh) and Fibroblast growth factor (Fgf) signaling regulate limb development in the axolotl. We found that Shh-expressing cells contributed to the most posterior digit, and that inhibiting Shh-signaling inhibited Fgf8 expression, anteroposterior patterning, and distal cell proliferation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that urodeles deviate from anurans and amniotes in exhibiting preaxial skeletal differentiation, contrasting with postaxial dominance in other tetrapods.

claim: Urodeles deviate from anurans and amniotes in that their limbs do not develop an apical ectodermal ridge (AER).
source: Here, we investigated how Sonic hedgehog (Shh) and Fibroblast growth factor (Fgf) signaling regulate limb development in the axolotl. We found that Shh-expressing cells contributed to the most posterior digit, and that inhibiting Shh-signaling inhibited Fgf8 expression, anteroposterior patterning, and distal cell proliferation. In addition to lack of a morphological AER, we found that salamander limbs also lack a molecular AER.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that urodeles do not develop an AER, which is a key difference from anurans and amniotes.

claim: Salamander limbs lack a molecular AER.
source: In addition to lack of a morphological AER, we found that salamander limbs also lack a molecular AER.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from the study.

claim: Amniote and anuran AER-specific Fgfs and their cognate receptors were expressed entirely in the mesenchyme in salamander limbs.
source: We found that amniote and anuran AER-specific Fgfs and their cognate receptors were expressed entirely in the mesenchyme.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding based on expression analysis.

claim: Fgf-signaling regulates cell proliferation across all three limb axes in salamanders.
source: Broad inhibition of Fgf-signaling demonstrated that this pathway regulates cell proliferation across all three limb axes, in contrast to anurans and amniotes where Fgf-signaling regulates cell survival and proximodistal patterning.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from Fgf inhibition experiments.

claim: In anurans and amniotes, Fgf-signaling regulates cell survival and proximodistal patterning.
source: Broad inhibition of Fgf-signaling demonstrated that this pathway regulates cell proliferation across all three limb axes, in contrast to anurans and amniotes where Fgf-signaling regulates cell survival and proximodistal patterning.
evidence: The abstract explicitly contrasts salamander Fgf function with that in anurans and amniotes, citing established knowledge.

claim: Shh-expressing cells contributed to the most posterior digit in axolotl limbs.
source: We found that Shh-expressing cells contributed to the most posterior digit, and that inhibiting Shh-signaling inhibited Fgf8 expression, anteroposterior patterning, and distal cell proliferation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from DiI labeling experiments.

claim: Inhibiting Shh-signaling inhibited Fgf8 expression in axolotl limbs.
source: We found that Shh-expressing cells contributed to the most posterior digit, and that inhibiting Shh-signaling inhibited Fgf8 expression, anteroposterior patterning, and distal cell proliferation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from cyclopamine treatment experiments.

claim: Inhibiting Shh-signaling inhibited anteroposterior patterning in axolotl limbs.
source: We found that Shh-expressing cells contributed to the most posterior digit, and that inhibiting Shh-signaling inhibited Fgf8 expression, anteroposterior patterning, and distal cell proliferation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from cyclopamine treatment experiments.

claim: Inhibiting Shh-signaling inhibited distal cell proliferation in axolotl limbs.
source: We found that Shh-expressing cells contributed to the most posterior digit, and that inhibiting Shh-signaling inhibited Fgf8 expression, anteroposterior patterning, and distal cell proliferation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from cyclopamine treatment experiments.

claim: Axolotl limb mesenchyme expanded directly above the body wall musculature during limb bud emergence.
source: As the limb bud emerged from the flank, limb mesenchyme expanded directly above the body wall musculature and at no time during limb development did we observe an AER or thickening of the limb ectoderm (Figure 1C).
evidence: The text explicitly describes this observation, supported by histological images in Figure 1C.

claim: At no time during axolotl limb development was an AER or thickening of the limb ectoderm observed.
source: As the limb bud emerged from the flank, limb mesenchyme expanded directly above the body wall musculature and at no time during limb development did we observe an AER or thickening of the limb ectoderm (Figure 1C).
evidence: The text explicitly states this observation, supported by histological images in Figure 1C.

claim: Cartilage condensations of the axolotl limb skeleton formed proximal to distal.
source: In agreement with previous work in salamanders (Holmgren, 1933; Nye et al., 2003; Shubin and Alberch, 1986), we found that cartilage condensations of the limb skeleton formed proximal to distal, and within the zeugopod and autopod, anterior to posterior (preaxial dominance) (Figure 1D).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding, supported by Alcian blue staining in Figure 1D and citing previous studies.

claim: Within the zeugopod and autopod, cartilage condensations formed anterior to posterior (preaxial dominance) in axolotl limbs.
source: In agreement with previous work in salamanders (Holmgren, 1933; Nye et al., 2003; Shubin and Alberch, 1986), we found that cartilage condensations of the limb skeleton formed proximal to distal, and within the zeugopod and autopod, anterior to posterior (preaxial dominance) (Figure 1D).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding, supported by Alcian blue staining in Figure 1D and citing previous studies.

claim: Alcian blue staining showed digit I and II forming together between stages 47 and 48 in axolotl limbs.
source: While this was strictly true for the radius and ulna, alcian blue staining always demonstrated digit I and II forming together between stages 47 and 48 (Figure 1D).
evidence: The text explicitly states this observation from Alcian blue staining shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Sox9 expression in presumptive digits appeared sequentially II-I-III-IV in 86.66% of axolotl limbs analyzed at stage 48.
source: However, in contrast to the Alcian blue staining pattern, Sox9 expression in the presumptive digits appeared sequentially II-I-III-IV and this result was consistent across 13/15 (86.66%) limbs analyzed across stage 48 (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding with specific quantification, supported by images in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Digit specification as marked by Sox9 expression in the axolotl autopod exhibits a pre-pattern that first emerges along the central axis marked by digit II.
source: Thus, although chondrification of the limb skeleton proceeds anterior to posterior in the zeugopod, digit specification as marked by Sox9 expression in the autopod exhibits a pre-pattern that first emerges along the central axis marked by digit II.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on Sox9 expression analysis.

claim: Shh was first expressed at stage 45 in a posteriorly restricted domain in axolotl forelimbs.
source: Using an antisense-probe (~1000 bp) that was a gift from the Tanaka lab (IMP, Austria), we determined that Shh was first expressed at stage 45 in a posteriorly restricted domain and persisted through stage 49 in a posterior-proximal position (Figure 2A).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Shh expression persisted through stage 49 in a posterior-proximal position in axolotl forelimbs.
source: Using an antisense-probe (~1000 bp) that was a gift from the Tanaka lab (IMP, Austria), we determined that Shh was first expressed at stage 45 in a posteriorly restricted domain and persisted through stage 49 in a posterior-proximal position (Figure 2A).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The onset of Shh expression in axolotls appeared relatively late and after Hoxd11 expression.
source: Compared to anuran and other amniote forelimb buds where Shh expression precedes expression of Hoxd11, the onset of Shh expression in axolotls appeared relatively late and after Hoxd11 expression (Matsubara et al., 2017; Riddle et al., 1993) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding, comparing to other tetrapods and citing references, with supporting data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Shh expression was observed in an anteriorly restricted domain at stages 46, 47 and 48 in axolotl forelimbs.
source: While the posterior Shh expression pattern was consistent with previous reports using relatively short probes at several stages (Bickelmann et al., 2018; Imokawa and Yoshizato, 1997; Torok et al., 1999), we also observed Shh expression in an anteriorly restricted domain at stages 46, 47 and 48 (Figure 2A).
evidence: The text explicitly states this novel finding from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2A.

claim: qRT-PCR showed Shh expression from both the anterior and posterior compartments of stage 46–49 axolotl limb buds.
source: To support our in situ data, we divided stage 46–49 limb buds into posterior and anterior halves and collected RNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C). Using qRT-PCR, we observed Shh expression from the anterior and posterior compartments (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The axolotl Shh RNA probe shared 42% similarity with Indian hedgehog (Ihh) sequences.
source: We also isolated full-length Indian hedgehog (Ihh) and aligned it with Shh revealing that our RNA probe shared 42% similarity between sequences (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Ihh expression was localized to areas of skeletal ossification in axolotl limbs.
source: Furthermore, we generated an RNA probe to Ihh and found spatiotemporal expression domains distinct from Shh expression localized to areas of skeletal ossification (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Posterior Shh expression in axolotl forelimb buds remains in a relatively small proximal domain rather than extending into the autopod.
source: Third, posterior Shh expression corresponding to the ZPA remains in a relatively small proximal domain (Torok et al., 1999) rather than the elongated expression domain found in other tetrapods that extends the proximal-distal length of the autopod (Matsubara et al., 2017; Riddle et al., 1993; Shapiro et al., 2003).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding, comparing to other tetrapods and citing references.

claim: DiI-labeled cells from the Shh domain migrated along the posterior limb margin and contributed to digit IV in axolotl limbs.
source: Although our injections labeled Shh-expressing cells and nearby cells as well, we only observed cells migrating along the posterior limb margin and contributing to digit IV (Figure 2E).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from DiI labeling experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: ZPA cells only give rise to the most posterior digit in the chick hindlimb and posterior margin of the forelimb.
source: This data mimics labeling experiments in chick limbs where ZPA cells only give rise to the most posterior digit in the hindlimb and posterior margin of the forelimb (Towers et al., 2008; Towers et al., 2011).
evidence: The text explicitly states this comparison to chick experiments, citing references.

claim: Fgf8, Fgf9 and Fgf17 were solely expressed in the mesenchyme of axolotl limb buds.
source: In contrast to anurans and amniotes, we found that Fgf8, Fgf9 and Fgf17 were solely expressed in the mesenchyme (Figure 3A–C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Fgf4 was not consistently detected during axolotl limb development, and when detected, was expressed at very low levels in the mesenchyme only.
source: We could not consistently detect Fgf4 during limb development and, when we did, it was expressed at very low levels in the mesenchyme only (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fgf8 was detected in a broad mesenchymal zone directly beneath the ectoderm at stage 44 in axolotl limbs.
source: At stage 44, we detected Fgf8 in a broad mesenchymal zone directly beneath the ectoderm (Figure 3A).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Fgf8 expression persisted in the distal mesenchyme until stage 47 when it segregated into symmetrical domains within the dorsal and ventral mesenchyme in axolotl limbs.
source: Fgf8 expression persisted in the distal mesenchyme until stage 47 when it segregated into symmetrical domains within the dorsal and ventral mesenchyme (Figure 3A–B).

claim: qRT-PCR showed Fgf8 expression in both the anterior and posterior compartment at stages 46, 47 and 49 in axolotl limbs.
source: Although Fgf8 appeared to exhibit an anteriorly restricted expression pattern at stage 44, using qRT-PCR we found Fgf8 expression in both the anterior and posterior compartment at stages 46, 47 and 49 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Fgf9 showed distally restricted expression at stages 45–46 in axolotl limbs.
source: Fgf9 and Fgf17 showed distally restricted expression at stages 45–46 and Fgf9 appeared to have an additional proximal expression domain at stage 46 (Figure 3C).

claim: Fgf9 appeared to have an additional proximal expression domain at stage 46 in axolotl limbs.
source: Fgf9 and Fgf17 showed distally restricted expression at stages 45–46 and Fgf9 appeared to have an additional proximal expression domain at stage 46 (Figure 3C).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Fgf17 showed distally restricted expression at stages 45–46 in axolotl limbs.
source: Fgf9 and Fgf17 showed distally restricted expression at stages 45–46 and Fgf9 appeared to have an additional proximal expression domain at stage 46 (Figure 3C).

claim: Fgf17 appeared to have a posterior bias at stage 46 in axolotl limbs.
source: Fgf17 appeared to have a posterior bias at stage 46 (Figure 3C).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Fgf10 was broadly expressed in the distal mesenchyme at stages 45–46 in axolotl limbs.

evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3C, comparing to other tetrapods.

claim: FgfR1 was first expressed weakly at stage 44 and became more proximally restricted during stages 45–46 in axolotl limbs.
source: FgfR1 was first expressed weakly at stage 44 and became more proximally restricted during stages 45–46 (Figure 3D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3D.

claim: At stage 46, the proximal-anterior domain of FgfR1 overlaps with the Fgf9 domain in axolotl limbs.
source: At stage 46, the proximal-anterior domain of FgfR1 overlaps with the Fgf9 domain (Figure 3C–D).

source: FgfR2 showed weak proximal expression at stage 44 and was later expressed during stages 45–46 in a domain proximal to Fgf8, 9 and 17 (Figure 3A–E and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3A-E.

claim: FgfR2 was expressed during stages 45–46 in a domain proximal to Fgf8, 9 and 17 in axolotl limbs.
source: FgfR2 showed weak proximal expression at stage 44 and was later expressed during stages 45–46 in a domain proximal to Fgf8, 9 and 17 (Figure 3A–E and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3A-E.

claim: Gremlin1 showed strong mesenchymal expression until digits began condensing at stage 48 in axolotl limbs.
source: Lastly, we examined Gremlin1 expression in developing salamander limbs, and observed strong mesenchymal expression until digits began condensing at stage 48 (Figure 3A).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Gremlin1 was detected at stage 49 in the area destined to become digits III and IV in axolotl limbs.
source: We also detected Gremlin1 staining at stage 49 in the area destined to become digits III and IV (Figure 3A).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Key Fgf ligands normally expressed in the ectoderm during amniote and anuran limb development are compartmentalized entirely in the limb mesenchyme in salamanders.
source: Taken together, our expression analysis shows that key Fgf ligands normally expressed in the ectoderm during amniote and anuran limb development are instead, compartmentalized entirely in the limb mesenchyme (Figure 3E).
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on expression analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Principal component 3 (PC3) models the proximodistal axis during stage 45 axolotl limb development based on known proximal and distal marker genes.
source: Using principal component analysis, we first identified principal component 3 (PC3) as a model for the proximodistal (P-D) axis during stage 45 based on known proximal and distal marker genes (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Proximal markers (Meis1 and Meis2) and distal markers (Fgf8 and Hoxd11) were expressed in cells on opposite ends of contributors to PC3 in stage 45 axolotl limbs.
source: Specifically, we found that proximal (Meis1 and Meis2) and distal markers (Fgf8 and Hoxd11) were expressed in cells on the opposite ends of contributors to PC3 (Figure 4A–B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Etv4 and Dusp6, which are direct targets of Fgf8, were among the top 20 genes contributing to the distal end of PC3 in stage 45 axolotl limbs.
source: Moreover, Etv4 and Dups6 which are direct targets of Fgf8 were among the top 20 genes contributing to the distal end (Hoxd11+) of PC3 (Figure 4A–B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fgf ligands (Fgf8, 9, 17 and 10) were all restricted to the distal end of PC3 in stage 45 axolotl limbs.
source: Consistent with expression patterns revealed by in situ hybridization, Fgf ligands such as Fgf8, 9, 17 and 10 were all restricted to the distal end of PC3, while Fgf receptors FgfR1-4 were restricted to the proximal end (Figure 4A–B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fgf receptors FgfR1-4 were restricted to the proximal end of PC3 in stage 45 axolotl limbs.
source: Consistent with expression patterns revealed by in situ hybridization, Fgf ligands such as Fgf8, 9, 17 and 10 were all restricted to the distal end of PC3, while Fgf receptors FgfR1-4 were restricted to the proximal end (Figure 4A–B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fgf ligands and Fgf receptors were statistically separated along PC3 in stage 45 axolotl limbs.
source: Statistical analysis confirmed that Fgf ligands (n = 12) and Fgf receptors (n = 5) were separated along PC3 (Welch Two Sample t-test, T = −4.1588, p=0.0038).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from statistical analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data.

claim: Some cells expressing FgfR1 in the distal portion of PC3 also expressed Fgf8, Fgf9 and Fgf17 in stage 45 axolotl limbs.
source: We also asked whether Fgf ligands and receptors might still be co-expressed in some cells and found that where FgfR1 was expressed in the distal portion of PC3, some of these cells also expressed Fgf8, Fgf9 and Fgf17 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from co-expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Few to no cells co-expressed FgfR2-4 and Fgf8, 9 and 17 in stage 45 axolotl limbs.
source: However, we found few to no cells co-expressing FgfR2-4 and Fgf8, 9 and 17 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from co-expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Limb buds harvested at stage 46 exhibited significantly smaller limbs following SU5402 treatment compared to control animals.
source: Limb buds harvested at stage 45 did not show a significant difference in limb size between treatment and control animals (one-tailed student's t-test, T = −1.68637, p=0.0514) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) whereas those harvested at stage 46 exhibited significantly smaller limbs (one-tailed student's t-test, T = −8.7759, p<0.0001) (Figure 5B).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from SU5402 treatment experiments with statistical analysis, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: SU5402 treatment led to a small, but significant decrease in total animal length (snout to tail-tip length).
source: Although we did find a small, but significant decrease in total animal length (snout to tail-tip length) following SU5402 treatment (one-tailed student's t-test, T = −4.52, p=0.0007) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), this did not account for the size differences between treatment and control limbs (T = −8.1, p<0.44).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from SU5402 treatment experiments with statistical analysis, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The decrease in total animal length following SU5402 treatment did not account for the size differences between treatment and control limbs.
source: Although we did find a small, but significant decrease in total animal length (snout to tail-tip length) following SU5402 treatment (one-tailed student's t-test, T = −4.52, p=0.0007) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), this did not account for the size differences between treatment and control limbs (T = −8.1, p<0.44).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from statistical analysis of SU5402 treatment experiments.

claim: Etv1 expression was undetectable in axolotl limb buds at stages 45 or 46 in response to Fgf inhibition with SU5402.
source: In response to Fgf inhibition, we were unable to detect Etv1 expression in the limb bud at stages 45 or 46 and Etv4 expression was barely detectable (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from in situ hybridization following SU5402 treatment, shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Etv4 expression was barely detectable in axolotl limb buds at stages 45 or 46 in response to Fgf inhibition with SU5402.
source: In response to Fgf inhibition, we were unable to detect Etv1 expression in the limb bud at stages 45 or 46 and Etv4 expression was barely detectable (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from in situ hybridization following SU5402 treatment, shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: qRT-PCR confirmed that Etv1 and Etv4 were significantly down-regulated at stage 46 following SU5402 treatment.
source: qRT-PCR confirmed that both targets were significantly down-regulated at stage 46 (Figure 5E).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from qRT-PCR analysis following SU5402 treatment, shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Shh expression was reduced in axolotl limb buds in response to Fgf inhibition with SU5402.
source: To determine if Fgf-signaling controls Shh-signaling, we quantified Shh expression in response to Fgf inhibition and found that it was reduced compared to control limbs (Figure 5E).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from qRT-PCR analysis following SU5402 treatment, shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Ptch1 expression was not reduced in SU5402-treated axolotl limb buds, suggesting that Shh pathway activity remained normal.
source: Given the relatively small number of Shh-expressing cells at these early time points, we asked if reduced Shh transcription translated into reduced pathway activity as assessed by Ptch1 expression (Figure 5E–G). Using qRT-PCR and in situ, we found that Ptch1 was not reduced in treated limb buds suggesting that Shh pathway activity remained normal (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from qRT-PCR and in situ hybridization following SU5402 treatment, shown in Figure 5E-G.

claim: Gremlin1 expression was virtually eliminated in SU5042-treated axolotl limbs.
source: Interestingly, while Gremlin1 is inhibited by AER-Fgf-signaling in amniotes (Merino et al., 1999; Verheyden and Sun, 2008), we found that Gremlin1 expression was virtually eliminated in SU5042-treated limbs (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from qRT-PCR and in situ hybridization following SU5402 treatment, shown in Figure 5E-G, contrasting with amniote findings.

claim: During normal axolotl limb development, no dying cells were detected using Lysotracker.
source: We used Lysotracker to mark dying cells (Mariani et al., 2008; Seifert et al., 2009) and during normal limb development we did not detect any dying cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from Lysotracker staining shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: When Fgf-signaling was inhibited with SU5402, no dying cells were detected in axolotl limb buds using Lysotracker.
source: Similarly, when we inhibited Fgf-signaling we did not detect dying cells in limb buds (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from Lysotracker staining following SU5402 treatment, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Inhibiting Fgf-signaling with SU5402 led to an 83% decrease in actively proliferating cells in stage 46 axolotl limb buds.
source: We calculated the proliferative population as a fraction of total limb volume and observed an 83% decrease in actively proliferating cells (one-way ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis test, p<0.05) (Figure 5I).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from EdU labeling and lightsheet microscopy following SU5402 treatment, shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The decrease in proliferating cells following SU5402 treatment appeared proportionally across the anteroposterior axis in axolotl limb buds.
source: While the decrease in proliferating cells appeared proportionally across the anteroposterior axis, we noted that proliferating cells were nearly absent from the proximal limb bud and from a small distal domain in treated limbs (Figure 5H).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from EdU labeling and lightsheet microscopy following SU5402 treatment, shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Proliferating cells were nearly absent from the proximal limb bud and from a small distal domain in SU5402-treated axolotl limbs.
source: While the decrease in proliferating cells appeared proportionally across the anteroposterior axis, we noted that proliferating cells were nearly absent from the proximal limb bud and from a small distal domain in treated limbs (Figure 5H).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from EdU labeling and lightsheet microscopy following SU5402 treatment, shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Inhibiting Fgf-signaling with SU5402 from before limb outgrowth until stage 54 led to smaller, but nearly complete limbs which generally lacked posterior digit IV.
source: Analyzing the forelimb skeleton, we found that inhibiting Fgf-signaling led to smaller, but nearly complete limbs which generally lacked posterior digit IV (Figure 5J–K).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from Alcian blue staining following SU5402 treatment, shown in Figure 5J-K.

claim: 73.5% of SU5402-treated embryos exhibited limbs lacking posterior digit IV.
source: Specifically, 73.5% of SU5402-treated embryos exhibited this phenotype (25/34) while ~11% (4/34) had fewer than three digits (Figure 5I).
evidence: The text explicitly states this quantification from SU5402 treatment experiments.

claim: In cases where more than one digit was lost following SU5402 treatment, the missing digits were the next most posterior in sequence.
source: In those cases where more than one digit was lost, the missing digits were the next most posterior in sequence.
evidence: The text explicitly states this observation from SU5402 treatment experiments.

claim: Fgf-signaling regulates mesenchymal proliferation, but not cell survival during axolotl limb development.
source: These results reveal that Fgf-signaling regulates mesenchymal proliferation, but not cell survival during axolotl limb development.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on SU5402 treatment experiments.

claim: Inhibiting Fgf-signaling leads to smaller limbs and loss of posterior digits in axolotls, a result consistent with colchicine treatment of developing axolotl and Xenopus larva.
source: Thus, inhibiting Fgf-signaling leads to smaller limbs and loss of posterior digits, a result consistent with colchicine treatment of developing axolotl and Xenopus larva (Alberch and Gale, 1983).
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion, comparing to previous colchicine experiments and citing a reference.

claim: Fgf-signaling regulates Gremlin1 expression during axolotl limb development.
source: Lastly, Fgf-signaling regulates Gremlin1 expression, whereas Shh-signaling is relatively independent of Fgf-signaling.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on SU5402 treatment experiments.

claim: Shh-signaling is relatively independent of Fgf-signaling during axolotl limb development.
source: Lastly, Fgf-signaling regulates Gremlin1 expression, whereas Shh-signaling is relatively independent of Fgf-signaling.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on SU5402 treatment experiments.

claim: Cyclopamine-treated axolotl limbs phenocopied Shh-/- mouse limbs with significant proximodistal outgrowth, fusion of the radius/ulna, and almost complete loss of the autopod.
source: Cyclopamine-treated axolotl limbs phenocopied Shh-/- mouse limbs with significant proximodistal outgrowth, fusion of the radius/ulna, and almost complete loss of the autopod (Chiang et al., 2001).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding, comparing to mouse Shh mutants and citing a reference.

claim: Limb buds from cyclopamine-treated larvae were significantly smaller compared to control treated limbs at stage 46.
source: Limb buds harvested at stage 45 did not show a significant difference in limb size between treatment and control animals (one-tailed student's t-test, T = 1.43, p=0.909) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), whereas at stage 46, limb buds from cyclopamine-treated larvae were significantly smaller compared to control treated limbs (one-tailed student's t-test, T = 8.36, p<0.0001) and this effect was independent of (T = 0.03, p=0.975) a small, but significant decrease in animal length (one-tailed student's t-test, T = 3.87, p<0.0016) (Figure 6B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from cyclopamine treatment experiments with statistical analysis, shown in Figure 6B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Cyclopamine treatment efficiently inhibited hedgehog signaling in axolotl limb buds as assessed by Ptch1 expression.
source: Analyzing Ptch1 expression by qRT-PCR and in situ hybridization, we found that cyclopamine treatment efficiently inhibited hedgehog signaling in limb buds (Figure 6C–E).
